The farewell dinner

Friday evening, the last week of September, in the flat in Cotroceni. Tomorrow morning Ioana flies to Japan. She came back a few days ago from Iași, where her mother taught her to make her grandmother’s ciorbă (Romanian sour soup), and she brought a pot of it for the farewell dinner. Mrs Doina has come too. Rosa Elena is sitting in her high chair.
(Tasting the ciorbă) Oh my…! Did you really make this yourself?
Yes. I learned it from my mother in Iași. It’s my grandmother’s recipe.
No wonder it’s so good. Maybe even better than mine. Though it annoys me to say so.
If Mrs Doina says so, it’s the real thing. That means you can make this taste in Kyoto too.
Have you finished packing?
Yes. But it went over twenty-three kilos… There’s no way I can leave Mrs Doina’s jam behind, so I took out two jumpers.
Oh dear, won’t you be cold without your jumpers?
It’s fine. I’ll wear the jumpers I wrapped the jars in once I’m there.
I see. So the jam is more important than the jumpers.
(Laughing) Ioana, we’re going to miss you.
…It’s not that I won’t miss you. But the excitement is bigger than the fear.
A year goes by in the blink of an eye. It’s not as if you’re leaving forever.
That’s right. And besides, we promised to talk on video every week, didn’t we?
Yes. If Rosa Elena forgets me, what will I do?
There’s no way she’ll forget you. This week, at last, she started talking.
What! Rozița? What did she say?
To me she said “agua” in Spanish, to Mihai “apă” in Romanian. Both mean “water”.
So she looks at who she’s talking to and chooses her language. If she was quiet for so long, it’s because she was listening.
Amazing! And Japanese?
When I sing her the lullaby, she says “nenne” (night-night).
(To Rosa Elena) Rozița, what about “Doina”? Go on, say “Doina”.
(Rosa Elena says “Na… na!” and points at Ioana) Oh! Was that for Ioana?
Me…? Is “Nana” my name?
(Laughing) So it wasn’t the “na” from Doina. Oh well. Today I’ll let you have it.
(Wiping away her tears) When someone calls your name on a night like this, how can you not cry…

wa-ke: two short, equal syllables, no long vowels. Don’t stretch it into “waake”. In ～わけ に は いかない, “ni wa” is said smoothly, without a pause: wa-ke-ni-wa i-ka-na-i (written に は, but は is read “wa”).
ku-ya-shi-i: four short syllables; at the end, two “i”s = one long “i” (“ya” is a separate syllable, not “kwai”). sha-be-ru: しゃ is a single syllable, the “r” a light tap.

na-ma-e: three syllables; “a” and “e” are said separately, not “nay”. chi-chi and ha-ha: equal syllables, like an echo. When you talk about someone else’s parents you say おとうさん (o-to-o-sa-n) and おかあさん (o-ka-a-sa-n), with long vowels.
1. ～わけ だ: “so”, “that means”, “that’s why”

At its root, わけ means “reason, meaning, explanation”. With だ at the end, ～わけ だ shows you’ve reached a CONCLUSION that follows naturally from what you know: “so…”, “that means…”, “well, that’s why…”. It doesn’t bring new information; it links two things so they make sense.
plain form + わけ だ
So you can make it in Kyoto too.
That’s why it’s good.
So the jam is more important.
な / である / という + わけ だ (not “の”!)
So he’s an only child.
past / negative
So it wasn’t the “na” from Doina.

Three typical situations: (1) with つまり or だから, to sum up: つまり、らいねん の くがつ まで いない わけ だ (so you won’t be here until next September). (2) with どうりで, when you find out the cause of something that surprised you: どうりで おいしい わけ だ (no wonder it’s good — you learned from your mother). (3) as a calm explanation, “that’s how things are”: あいて を みて、ことば を えらんで いる わけ です (so she looks at who she’s talking to and chooses her language).

Don’t confuse わけ だ with はず だ (ch. 41). はず = what you EXPECT to be the case, before checking (“it should arrive today”). わけ = what you UNDERSTAND once you’ve found out the reason (“aha, that’s why it didn’t arrive”). With どうりで both work: どうりで おいしい はず だ / わけ だ — with わけ it sounds more like “now I get it”.

English has lots of spoken equivalents: “so”, “that’s why”, “that means”, “no wonder”, “of course”. Whenever in English you’d say “aha, so then…”, in Japanese you almost certainly have ～わけ だ (polite ～わけ です; in speech often ～わけ ね or, when you’ve only just worked it out, ～わけ か).
2. ～わけ では ない / ～わけ じゃ ない: “it’s not exactly that…”

The negative ～わけ では ない (spoken: ～わけ じゃ ない) doesn’t deny the fact, but a CONCLUSION the other person might draw: “it doesn’t mean that…”, “it’s not really the case that…”. It’s a soft, partial negation — very Japanese.
It’s not as if you’re leaving forever. (it doesn’t mean you’ll disappear)
It’s not that I understand all of the Japanese. (I only understand part of it)
It’s not that I won’t miss you. (in fact I’ll miss you a bit)
It’s not that I don’t like it, but every day is a bit much…

The double negative ～ない わけ では ない (“it’s not that … not”) means a shy, half-hearted “yes”: さびしく ない わけ では ない = I do miss you a little, but I don’t want to make a fuss. It’s often followed by けど / が with the real point: …でも、たのしみ の ほう が 大きい.

With ぜんぶ, いつも, みんな, かならず, ～わけ では ない makes a partial negation: みんな が やさしい わけ では ない (not everyone is kind — some are, some aren’t). It’s the same in English: “not everyone” versus “no one”. You’ll come back to it in ch. 82, together with ～とは かぎらない.
3. ～わけ が ない / ～わけ ない: “there’s no way…”, “out of the question”
～わけ が ない firmly rejects a possibility: “there’s no reason at all for…” = “there’s no way…”, “impossible”. It attaches just like わけ だ (な-adj. + な, noun + な / である). In speech, が drops: わすれる わけ ない よ.

In many sentences both work. The difference is mostly one of tone: はず が ない is a detective’s reasoning, わけ が ない is a friend’s outburst: “No way!”.

Don’t mix up ～わけ が ない (“there’s no way”) with ～わけ では ない (“it’s not exactly that”). わすれる わけ が ない = she definitely WON’T forget. わすれる わけ では ない = it’s not that she forgets (it’s something else). A single particle changes the whole meaning.
4. ～わけ に は いかない: “I can’t, it wouldn’t be right” (and ～ない わけ に は いかない: “I must”)

This isn’t about being physically UNABLE, but about it NOT BEING RIGHT: the situation, your conscience or your relationship with others won’t allow it: “there’s no way I can…”, “I can’t afford to…”. It goes after the dictionary form.

And in everyday speech: わけ on its own, as a noun, means “reason”: わけ を きかせて (tell me the reason), わけ が わからない (I don’t understand at all, “it makes no sense”). That’s how you remember the whole family: everything starts from “reason / meaning”.
Reread the dialogue and put your finger on every わけ. Which is a conclusion, which a soft negation, which an “out of the question!”, which an “it wouldn’t be right”? There are ten in total.
6. Kanji: 言 名 前 子 父 母 (+ 語)

Around the middle of September, Ioana went home to Iași. In the kitchen her mother was waiting for her, apron on.
“Ciorbă, you know, can’t be made in a hurry. Give the soup time.”
The two of them spent a whole day in the kitchen. Ioana wrote down in her notebook everything her mother said.
“Do you remember how Grandma used to make you eat ciorbă, whether you wanted to or not?” her mother laughed. “I remember. Back then I couldn’t stand it, and now it’s my favourite. Strange, isn’t it?”
“There’s nothing strange about it. Grandma knew that. That’s why she made it every week.”
Then she translated the recipe into Japanese. So that Mrs Fumiko could read it too, in Kyoto.
In the evening her mother tasted it and said quietly: “Yes. That’s Grandma’s taste. Like this, you can make it anywhere.”
Her father, as usual, said nothing. But before going to bed he knocked on the door of Ioana’s room.
In his hand he had two small clocks. One was set to Romanian time, the other to Japanese time.
“The one on Romanian time is for you. The one on Japanese time I’ll hang on the kitchen wall. I’m not going to ring you while you’re asleep, am I.”
Ioana hugged her father from behind. It seemed to her that his back was a little smaller than it used to be.
“…Look after your health.” That was all her father said, and he quietly closed the door.
The morning after Ioana got back to Bucharest, it happened. When Ana picked up a glass, Rosa Elena pointed at it and said: “Agua!”
It’s “water” in Spanish. Ana nearly dropped the glass. “Did she… just talk?”
That evening, when Mihai came home from the hospital, Rosa Elena pointed at the same glass and said: “Apa!” This time it was “water” in Romanian.
Mihai stood there open-mouthed for a while. “Romanian for me, Spanish for Ana… That means she knows perfectly well who speaks which language.”
When he sang her the lullaby before bed, Rosa Elena said in a sleepy voice: “Nenne.” Her third word was in Japanese.
In fact, because the words just wouldn’t come, Ana had been a little worried. But Mihai, as a doctor, knew.
“Children who grow up surrounded by several languages sometimes start talking a little later. It’s not that she was simply silent. She was listening all the time, to all three.”
The next day at lunchtime, when she heard the story, Elena looked a little put out. “I come every day and she still doesn’t say ‘buni’ (Granny)?”
From then on Elena started repeating “buni, buni” to Rosa Elena goodness knows how many times a day.
At the farewell dinner on Friday evening, Rosa Elena pointed at Ioana and called her “Nana”. That became Ioana’s new name.
Mrs Doina pretended to be put out — “And there I was thinking it was the ‘na’ from Doina!” — and made everyone laugh.
On Saturday morning Otopeni airport was still dark, and beyond the glass the lights of the planes were shining.
Ioana’s father and mother had come from Iași on the night train. Mrs Doina said too: “There’s no way I’m not coming to see her off”, and came in Mr Petre’s car.
Mr Petre gave her a bone-shaped keyring: “From our dog.”
When they put the suitcase on the scales, it weighed exactly twenty-three kilos. “So you took out as many jumpers as the jam weighs”, Mrs Doina laughed proudly.
They checked in the luggage and went as far as the gate. Her mother held Ioana in her arms for a long time and wouldn’t let go.
Her father again said just one thing: “I’ll be watching the kitchen clock, you know.”
Mihai said: “When you’re in trouble, look at the card. And if that still doesn’t help, call me, don’t worry about the time.”
Ana said: “Give my regards to Mrs Fumiko. And make sure you eat properly!” and straightened Ioana’s scarf.
Finally, Ioana crouched down in front of Rosa Elena. “Rosa Elena, see you soon.”
Then Rosa Elena grabbed her finger and said clearly: “Nana, see you soon.”
Everyone looked at each other. It was the first time she had put two words together. And in Japanese, no less.
“Because every Saturday, when I left, I used to say ‘see you soon’ to her… she remembered.”
Ioana was laughing and crying at the same time. “There’s no way we’ll forget each other. Neither me, nor you, Rosa Elena.”
Ioana turned round again and again and waved. Then she disappeared beyond the gate.
After one change of plane, she arrived at Kansai airport on Sunday morning, Japan time.
On the train to Kyoto, Ioana took out Mihai’s card. When she turned it over, she saw something written in small letters on the back.
“For Nana. When you’re in trouble, look at this card. We’re always here. Mihai and Ana”
Underneath was a scribbled circle in blue crayon. Rosa Elena’s signature.
When she came out through the ticket gates at Kyoto station, there stood a small old lady holding a big sheet of paper.
“Welcome. …You kept your promise.” Mrs Fumiko, too, remembered that “I will certainly come” from Bucharest.
Ioana was close to tears and could barely get the words out: “I’m home… I mean no, nice to meet you… not that either…” Mrs Fumiko laughed: “Either one is fine.”
Mrs Fumiko asked a student who was passing by to take a photo of the two of them.
In Bucharest it was still early on Sunday morning. In the photo that arrived on Mihai’s phone, Mrs Fumiko and Ioana stood side by side, holding the big sheet of paper.
The sheet said “Welcome”. “Oh, it’s like the sheet I held at the airport in Bucharest!” Mihai laughed.
At lunchtime a video call came from Kyoto. It was already evening there. In the room at the back of the teahouse, Ioana and Mrs Fumiko sat side by side.
Mrs Fumiko opened Mrs Doina’s jar and spread a generous amount on bread. “I was told very firmly not to put it in my tea, you see.”
When Ana hurried to fetch Mrs Doina from next door, she laughed loudly in front of the screen: “That’s it, on bread!”
Rosa Elena copied her and said: “Pan!” In Spanish and in Japanese alike, bread is “pan”.
When Ioana’s face appeared on the screen, Rosa Elena patted the screen with her hands and shouted: “Nana!”
“Oh my, Hana-chan is talking! ‘Nana’ is Ioana, isn’t it?” “Yes. It’s my dearest name, the one Rosa Elena gave me.”
Meanwhile, on the wall of a kitchen in Iași, a small clock was quietly ticking, six hours ahead.

Since Rosa Elena was born, Ana has kept a diary in Japanese, to read to her one day. Here is the page from the last day of September. Find all the forms with わけ and the new kanji (言, 名, 前, 子, 父, 母).
Last day of September, clear skies. I’m writing down here the little one’s first words.
To me “agua”, to Mihai “apa”, to the lullaby “nenne”.
Her first name wasn’t “mama” or “dada”, but “Nana”. It stings a little, but if it’s Ioana, I can’t complain.
Elena still hasn’t managed to get her to say “buni”. So she says “buni, buni” to her every day.
I was worried because she was late to talk, but it wasn’t that she was silent. So she was listening all along.
Until the day the little one reads this notebook, I’ll keep writing. There’s no way I can stop.

Write 8–10 sentences about a farewell in your life (a friend who moved away, leaving to study, a holiday that ended). What did you feel? What did you only understand later? What would it not have been right to do? What could you never forget?
I used ～わけ だ for a conclusion (with つまり or どうりで).
I used ～わけ では ない for a soft negation (or ～ない わけ では ない).
I used ～わけ が ない for something impossible.
I used ～わけ に は いかない or ～ない わけ に は いかない.
I wrote at least two words in kanji: 言う, 名前, 前, 子, 父, 母.
When I was in secondary school, my best friend moved to Germany.
It’s not that I didn’t miss her, but I thought it wouldn’t be right to cry.
At the airport, my friend said: “We’ll definitely see each other again, right?”
Ten years have passed since then. We still talk every month. So distance doesn’t matter.
There’s no way I could forget that day.
Listen to the dialogue 3 times. Every time you hear わけ, stop and say in English what it does: conclusion, soft negation, “out of the question!” or “it wouldn’t be right / I must”.
